meta.title: Bursty errors: a two-state Markov (Gilbert–Elliott) channel
meta.tools: Two-state Markov chain simulation, stationary distribution, burst-length statistics, block-error rates with and without interleaving, comparison with an i.i.d. channel of equal average BER
meta.summary: Model a channel that alternates between good and bad states, predict its average error rate and burst-length distribution from the transition probabilities, and show that a block code that fixes 2 errors fails far more often on bursty errors — until interleaving spreads them out.
meta.problem: Fading and interference produce errors in clumps. Why does the average bit-error rate say so little about how a code will perform?
meta.theory:
States G/B with P(G→B) = p, P(B→G) = q: stationary π_B = p/(p+q); average BER = π_G e_G + π_B e_B. Sojourn in B is geometric with mean 1/q. For a t-error-correcting block code of length n, block failure = P(>t errors);
on an i.i.d. channel this is a binomial tail, on the bursty channel much larger for the same average BER. Interleaving to depth D ≫ 1/q makes errors within a codeword nearly independent.
meta.method: p = 0.002, q = 0.1, e_G = 10⁻⁴, e_B = 0.3 (average BER ≈ 0.6 %). 10⁷ simulated bits. Codewords of n = 63 correcting t = 2 errors (BCH-like); block failure rates: bursty, bursty + interleaving (depth 64), i.i.d. with the same BER.
